title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: The rain didn't last long, and by the time Vronsky arrived — his shaft horse trotting at full speed, dragging the trace horses at a gallop through the mud, their reins hanging loose — the sun had peeked out again, and the roofs of the summer villas and the old lime trees in the gardens along both sides of the main street sparkled with wet brilliance, and from the twigs came a pleasant drip and from the roofs water poured in rushing streams. He no longer thought about the rain ruining the racecourse; he was glad now that — thanks to the rain — he was sure to find her at home and alone, since he knew that Alexey Alexandrovitch, just back from a foreign watering place, had not budged from Petersburg.

Hoping to find her alone, Vronsky got out, as he always did, before crossing the bridge, to avoid attracting attention, and walked the rest of the way to the house. He did not go up the steps to the front door, but went round to the courtyard.
"Has your master come?" he asked a gardener.
"No, sir. The mistress is at home. But please go to the front door — there are servants there," the gardener answered. "They'll open it for you."
"No, I'll go in from the garden."

Satisfied that she was alone, and wanting to surprise her — since he hadn't promised to come today, and she would surely not expect him before the races — he walked, holding his sword and stepping carefully along the sandy path bordered with flowers, toward the terrace looking out over the garden. Vronsky forgot now everything he had been thinking on the way about the hardships and difficulties of their position. He thought only of how he was about to see her, not in his imagination, but living, all of her, as she really was. He was just going in, planting his foot flat on each tread so as not to make the worn steps of the terrace creak, when he suddenly remembered what he always forgot, and what made the most painful side of his relations with her — her son with his questioning eyes, hostile, as Vronsky imagined them.

This boy was, more than anyone else, a check on their freedom. When he was around, both Vronsky and Anna not only avoided talking about anything they couldn't have said in front of everyone — they didn't even allow themselves to refer by hints to anything the boy didn't understand. They had made no agreement about this; it had settled itself. They would have felt it shameful to lie to the child. In his presence they spoke like acquaintances. But in spite of this caution, Vronsky often caught the child's intent, bewildered glance fixed on him, and noticed a strange shyness, uncertainty — sometimes friendliness, sometimes coldness and reserve — in the boy's manner toward him, as if the child sensed that between this man and his mother there was some important bond whose meaning he could not grasp.

In fact the boy did feel that he couldn't understand this connection, and he tried painfully, and could not manage, to work out what he was supposed to feel for this man. With a child's keen instinct for every shade of feeling, he saw clearly that his father, his governess, his nurse — all of them not only disliked Vronsky but looked on him with horror and revulsion, though they never said a word about him — while his mother regarded him as her greatest friend.

"What does it mean? Who is he? How am I supposed to love him? If I don't know, it's my fault — either I'm stupid or a bad boy," thought the child. And that was what produced the doubtful, questioning, sometimes hostile expression, and the shyness and uncertainty that Vronsky found so unbearable. This child's presence always and infallibly stirred up in Vronsky that strange feeling of inexplicable loathing he had been having lately. The child's presence aroused in both Vronsky and Anna a feeling like that of a sailor who sees by the compass that the direction in which he is moving rapidly is far from the right one, but knows it isn't in his power to stop, that every instant is carrying him further off, and that to admit to himself his deviation from the right course is the same as admitting his certain ruin.
This child, with his innocent view of the world, was the compass that showed them how far they had strayed from what they knew but did not want to know.

This time Seryozha was not at home, and she was completely alone. She was sitting on the terrace waiting for the return of her son, who had gone out for a walk and been caught in the rain. She had sent a manservant and a maid out to look for him. Wearing a white gown with deep embroidery, she was sitting in a corner of the terrace behind some flowers, and didn't hear him. With her curly black head bent, she pressed her forehead against a cool watering pot that stood on the parapet, and both of her lovely hands, with the rings he knew so well, clasped the pot. The beauty of her whole figure, her head, her neck, her hands, struck Vronsky each time as something new and unexpected. He stood still, gazing at her in ecstasy. But the moment he took a step toward her, she sensed his presence, pushed the watering pot away, and turned her flushed face to him.

"What's the matter? Are you ill?" he said to her in French, going up to her. He would have run to her, but, remembering that there might be people watching, he glanced toward the balcony door and flushed a little, as he always did when feeling that he had to be afraid and on his guard.
"No, I'm quite well," she said, getting up and pressing his outstretched hand tightly. "I didn't expect... thee."
"Mercy — what cold hands!" he said.
"You startled me," she said. "I'm alone, waiting for Seryozha; he's out for a walk; they'll be coming in from this side."
But for all her efforts to be calm, her lips were trembling.

"Forgive me for coming, but I couldn't get through the day without seeing you," he went on, speaking French, as he always did, to avoid the stiff Russian plural form, so impossibly cold between them, and the dangerously intimate singular.
"Forgive you? I'm so glad you're here!"
"But you're ill or troubled," he went on, still holding her hands and bending over her. "What were you thinking about?"
"Always the same thing," she said with a smile.

She was telling the truth. If at any moment she had been asked what she was thinking about, she could have answered honestly: of the same thing — of her happiness and her unhappiness. She was thinking, just as he came upon her, of this: why, she wondered, was it that for others, for Betsy (she knew about her secret affair with Tushkevitch), it was all easy, while for her it was such torture? Today this thought had taken on particular sharpness from certain other things. She asked him about the races. He answered her questions, and, seeing that she was agitated, trying to calm her, he began to tell her in the most matter-of-fact tone the details of his preparations for the races.

"Tell him or not tell him?" she thought, looking into his quiet, affectionate eyes. "He is so happy, so absorbed in his races, that he won't understand the way he ought, he won't understand all the weight of this fact for us."
"But you haven't told me what you were thinking about when I came in," he said, breaking off his story. "Please tell me!"

She didn't answer, and, bowing her head a little, she looked at him questioningly from under her brows, her eyes shining beneath their long lashes. Her hand shook as it played with a leaf she had picked. He saw it, and his face took on that look of utter surrender, of slavish devotion, that had done so much to win her.
"I can see something has happened. Do you suppose I can be at peace knowing you have a trouble I'm not sharing? Tell me, for God's sake," he repeated imploringly.

"Yes, I won't be able to forgive him if he doesn't realize all the seriousness of it. Better not tell — why put him to the test?" she thought, still staring at him in the same way, and feeling the hand holding the leaf was trembling more and more.
"For God's sake!" he repeated, taking her hand.
"Shall I tell you?"
"Yes, yes, yes...."

"I am with child," she said, softly and deliberately. The leaf in her hand shook more violently, but she did not take her eyes off him, watching to see how he would take it. He went pale, was about to say something, and stopped; he dropped her hand, and his head sank on his chest. "Yes, he realizes all the gravity of it," she thought, and she pressed his hand gratefully.

But she was wrong to think he realized the gravity of the fact as she, a woman, realized it. On hearing it, he felt that strange feeling of loathing for someone come over him with ten times the force. But at the same time he felt that the turning point he had been longing for had now arrived; that it was no longer possible to keep things from her husband, and that, one way or another, they would soon have to put an end to their unnatural position. Beyond that, her emotion physically affected him in the same way it had affected her. He looked at her with a look of submissive tenderness, kissed her hand, got up, and silently paced up and down the terrace.

"Yes," he said, going up to her firmly. "Neither you nor I have looked on our relations as a passing amusement, and now our fate is decided. We absolutely must put an end" — he glanced around as he spoke — "to the deception we are living in."
"Put an end? How put an end, Alexey?" she said softly.
She was calmer now, and her face lit up with a tender smile.
"Leave your husband and let us make our life one."
"It is one as it is," she answered, barely audibly.
"Yes — but altogether; altogether."
"But how, Alexey, tell me how?" she said in melancholy mockery at the hopelessness of her own position. "Is there any way out of such a position? Am I not my husband's wife?"

"There is a way out of every position. We have to take our course," he said. "Anything is better than the position you're living in. Of course I see how you torture yourself over everything — the world, your son, your husband."
"Oh, not over my husband," she said with a quiet smile. "I don't know him, I don't think of him. He doesn't exist."
"You're not being honest. I know you. You worry about him too."

"Oh, he doesn't even know," she said, and suddenly a hot flush spread across her face; her cheeks, her brow, her neck went crimson, and tears of shame came into her eyes. "But we won't talk about him."
